guideTitle: 6 Best Small Rain Barrels with Spigot in 2026
metaTitle: Best Small Rain Barrels with Spigot (2026)
metaDescription: Six compact rain barrels with spigots compared on capacity, collapsible vs rigid design, overflow, and how easy each is to fill a watering can from.
introParagraphs: A small rain barrel sounds simple, yet the word small covers everything from a bucket-style catcher to a 50 gallon drum that still fits beside a downspout. What really separates the options is not the headline capacity but the spigot, the overflow, and whether the barrel folds flat or stands as a rigid shell. A spigot that sits too low to slide a watering can under it will frustrate you every week of the season.

We evaluated six rain barrels that pair a spigot with a compact footprint, based on product specs and buyer feedback on the listings. The lineup runs from the Japard 16 inch slim 26 gallon tank to the RTS Home Accents 50 gallon flat back barrels, with collapsible PVC models from VINGLI and Laspeiraux in between. Each one trades capacity, storage convenience, and sturdiness in a different way.

Rain barrel water is for plants, lawns, and washing the car, not for drinking or cooking. Whichever size you pick, plan the overflow path and keep a fine screen over every opening so mosquitoes cannot use it as a nursery.

products.name: RTS Home Accents 50-Gallon Rain Barrel, Brass Spigot (Walnut)
products.description:
The Walnut RTS barrel is a rigid 50 gallon polyethylene drum with a flat back, so it sits snug against a wall or downspout without wasting the strip of ground beside it. The brass spigot is a real advantage over the plastic taps on many small barrels, because brass threads stay tight through repeated hose connections. A built-in overflow valve handles excess water once the barrel is full, and the listing says you can connect multiple barrels for more storage.

At 50 gallons it is the largest solid barrel in this lineup, which means it is only small by rain barrel standards. The UV-resistant polyethylene is meant to survive years of sun, but a rigid shell cannot be folded away for winter, so you need a spot for it or a plan to drain and tip it. A full barrel of this size is heavy, so it needs level, firm ground.

Day to day, the work is light: check the screen for leaves, open the spigot, and fill the can. The spigot sits low unless you raise the barrel on blocks, so budget for a stand if you want to fit a tall watering can underneath. Compared with the Japard at 26 gallons, the RTS holds nearly twice as much, and compared with the collapsible Laspeiraux at 53 gallons it offers a firmer, more upright body that does not bulge as it fills.

products.name: RTS Home Accents 50-Gallon ECO Rain Barrel
products.description:
The ECO version of the RTS barrel is made from 100% recycled plastic and shares the 50 gallon capacity and flat back profile of the Walnut model. The listing highlights UV-resistant polyethylene and a built-in overflow valve, with the option to connect several barrels together. For buyers who care where the plastic came from, this is the one that says so on the product page.

The tradeoff against the Walnut model is the spigot: the ECO listing does not mention brass, so check what ships with it before assuming the same long-life tap. Like every rigid barrel here it needs space year round, and it cannot be packed away the way the collapsible VINGLI can. Its flat back makes it a good fit for narrow side yards.

Setup means cutting or diverting the downspout, leveling the base, and screening the opening. Fill and drain are as simple as the other RTS barrel, and at 50 gallons it holds slightly less than the 53 gallon Laspeiraux while being far more stable when full. If you want the same footprint as the Walnut barrel with a recycled-plastic story, this is the match.

products.name: VINGLI PVC Collapsible Rain Barrel, 50 Gallon, Green

specList.label: Sealing
specList.value: Double rings on spigot and outflow valve

products.description:
The VINGLI is a foldable PVC rain barrel rated at 50 gallons, built on sturdy PVC support frames that the listing describes as winter-ready and crackproof. Each spigot and outflow valve pairs with a double sealing ring system, a detail aimed squarely at the slow drips that plague cheap collapsible barrels. It catches water from a gutter downspout and folds away when the season ends.

The tradeoff of any collapsible design is that the walls flex as the barrel fills, so it needs a flat, debris-free base and some care near sharp edges. It will not look as polished as a molded drum, and the spigot sits low unless you elevate it. Buyers who garden in cold climates will like that it packs flat and does not have to be dragged into a garage in one heavy piece.

Ownership is mostly about setup and storage: connect it to the downspout, check the sealing rings after the first fill, and fold it clean and dry at season end. Its 50 gallons match the RTS barrels, while the Japard at 26 gallons is the leaner option and the Laspeiraux at 53 gallons adds a little more volume with a different faucet design. For small-space gardeners who value storage over looks, this is the safest collapsible pick.

products.name: Laspeiraux Collapsible Rain Barrel, 53 Gallon
products.description:
The Laspeiraux holds 53 gallons in a three-layer PVC body that folds for storage and carrying. Its headline feature is an integrated design with a straightforward screw-in faucet, which the maker presents as a fix for the leaks that come from the separate fittings on many barrels. That makes installation less fiddly than a drill-and-bulkhead kit.

As the largest barrel in this comparison by raw volume, it pushes the definition of small, but its collapsible shape means it takes almost no room when empty. The compromise is the same as the VINGLI: soft walls rely on a flat, level base and a clean surface under the barrel. Anyone who wants a rigid, wall-hugging shape will prefer the RTS.

At home you screw in the faucet, set the barrel on blocks, and direct the downspout in. After the season, drain it, let it dry, and fold it down. Next to the VINGLI at 50 gallons it offers 3 more gallons and a simpler faucet, while the Japard at 26 gallons is the better pick for tight corners. For buyers who dread plumbing work, the integrated faucet is the draw.

products.name: Japard 16 Inch Slim Collapsible Rain Barrel, 26 Gallon
products.description:
The Japard is the slimmest option here, a 16 inch wide collapsible tank listed at 26 gallons and designed to take water from a gutter. The narrow profile is the point: it slides into corners, balconies, and side-of-house gaps where a 50 gallon drum would never fit. The listing also says it works indoors or outdoors.

The cost of that slim shape is capacity. At 26 gallons it holds about half of what the RTS or VINGLI barrels hold, so it fills fast in a storm and the overflow path needs attention. Like the other collapsible barrels it relies on soft walls, so give it a flat base and check it after heavy fills.

Day to day, it is the easiest to place and the easiest to put away. Fold it, shelve it, and bring it out in spring. Compared with the Laspeiraux at 53 gallons it covers less volume, but it fits places that bigger barrels simply cannot. For a balcony herb garden or a few raised pots, 26 gallons goes further than people expect.

products.description:
The WRUIOY is a portable, bucket-style rain catcher with a wide mouth, a mesh cover, a PVC frame, and spigots. The listing is titled with a 2 6 gallon capacity, so confirm the exact size on the product page before ordering. Each outlet and valve uses two rubber rings, which is the maker's answer to leaks.

Its wide mouth makes it a catcher you can place under a roof edge or a short downspout, rather than a tank you plumb into a gutter. That makes it the smallest and most flexible pick here, but also the one with the least stored water per storm. Do not expect it to carry a whole vegetable bed.

Use is straightforward: set it out, check the mesh cover, and open the spigot. Compared with the Japard at 26 gallons it is a much lighter commitment, and against the RTS at 50 gallons it is an entry point rather than a long-term solution. For potted plants and a patio, it is enough.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Capacity decides how long a dry week your garden can ride out. A 26 gallon barrel like the Japard covers a few containers, while the 50 gallon RTS and VINGLI barrels and the 53 gallon Laspeiraux handle a small raised bed. A rule of thumb is that a single watering of a 4 by 8 foot bed uses a good fraction of 50 gallons, so do not undersize if you garden in beds. If you only water pots, the 26 gallon Japard is plenty and easier to place.

The spigot is the part you use every week, so it deserves attention. The RTS Walnut barrel uses a brass spigot, which resists thread wear better than plastic, while the Laspeiraux uses an integrated screw-in faucet. Low spigots will not clear a standard watering can, so plan on blocks or a stand that lift the barrel at least a foot. Ask whether the faucet can take a garden hose adapter if you plan to drip irrigate.

Collapsible PVC barrels like the VINGLI at 50 gallons and the Laspeiraux at 53 gallons fold flat for winter and cost you little storage space. Rigid polyethylene barrels like the RTS ECO hold their shape and sit flush to a wall, but they take space year round. In freezing climates, being able to fold a barrel away after draining it is a real benefit. If you have a shed with no spare floor, choose collapsible.

A small barrel fills in minutes during a storm, and the overflow must go somewhere safe. The RTS barrels list a built-in overflow valve and multi-barrel connection, which helps if you later add a second 50 gallon unit. Direct any overflow away from the foundation. If your barrel has no overflow outlet, keep the downspout diverter easy to reconnect.

Standing water attracts mosquitoes, which need several days to mature, so a tight lid and fine mesh over every opening matter. The WRUIOY ships with a mesh cover over its wide mouth, and the RTS barrels list screens on the barrel tops in related models. Clean the screen after storms, particularly under trees. A clogged screen sends water over the sides and may clog the spigot.

A full 50 gallon barrel weighs over 400 pounds, so base matters as much as size. The RTS flat back shape and the Japard 16 inch slim profile solve different footprint problems, one against a wall and the other in a narrow gap. Set any barrel on level, firm blocks or pavers, never on bare soil. For collapsible barrels, add a smooth pad so sharp stones cannot puncture the PVC.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity versus footprint
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated capacity against how much space each barrel takes up. The Japard at 26 gallons and 16 inches wide leads on tight fits, while the 53 gallon Laspeiraux leads on volume. We treated a barrel as small only when its footprint was manageable for a side yard or balcony.

howWeEvaluated.title: Spigot and fittings
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at what each listing says about the spigot, seals, and faucet. The RTS Walnut brass spigot, the VINGLI double sealing rings, and the Laspeiraux integrated faucet each address leaks differently. Picks with clearer leak-prevention features scored higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Rigid versus collapsible build
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed the sturdiness of rigid polyethylene against the storage convenience of PVC. The RTS ECO and Walnut barrels lead on stability when full, while the VINGLI and Laspeiraux lead on folding away. Each trade was noted rather than ranked as simply better.

howWeEvaluated.title: Overflow, screening, and water safety
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked for overflow valves, mesh screens, and lids described in the listings. The RTS barrels list built-in overflow and the WRUIOY lists a mesh cover. Picks without a stated overflow were marked as needing a separate plan.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of daily use
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how simple installation and weekly use appear to be based on product specs and buyer feedback. The Laspeiraux screw-in faucet and the WRUIOY wide mouth keep setup simple, while the 50 gallon barrels need a stand for comfortable watering can access.

faq.q: What counts as a small rain barrel?
faq.a: In this comparison, small means a footprint a side yard or balcony can handle, from the 26 gallon Japard up to 50 and 53 gallon barrels. Capacity alone does not decide it; a 16 inch slim profile can be smaller in practice than a flat back drum. Pick based on the space you have and the area you water.

faq.q: How many gallons do I need?
faq.a: For a handful of pots, 26 gallons from the Japard is usually enough. For a small raised bed, aim for 50 gallons like the RTS or VINGLI. A barrel fills fast during a storm, so overflow handling matters as much as volume.

Collapsible barrels such as the VINGLI use PVC support frames and sealing rings, and the Laspeiraux uses a three-layer PVC body. They work well on a flat, clean base and are easy to store. Rigid polyethylene like the RTS barrels is steadier when full, so choose by how you want to store it.

faq.q: Can I drink the water from a rain barrel?
faq.a: No. Roof runoff is for plants, lawns, and washing, not for drinking or cooking. Keep the barrel covered and screened so debris and mosquitoes stay out.

Keep a tight lid and a fine mesh screen over every opening, because mosquitoes need several days of standing water to mature. The WRUIOY ships with a mesh cover. Check the screen after storms and clear any leaves.

faq.q: Do I need to winterize a rain barrel?
faq.a: In freezing climates, drain the barrel fully, leave the spigot open, and reconnect the downspout. Collapsible models like the VINGLI and Laspeiraux fold away easily after draining, while rigid RTS barrels should be tipped or stored. Ice can crack fittings.

faq.q: Why is my spigot too low?
faq.a: Most small barrels place the tap near the bottom to drain as much water as possible. Raise the barrel on blocks or pavers by about a foot so a watering can fits. Make sure the base is level and firm before you fill it.
